props.title: How the space sounds
props.seo_title: How the space sounds: volume, echo, power and the toast microphone
props.dek: Most of what goes wrong with live music at an event starts in the space, before anyone plays a note. Volume, frequency, echo, wattage, microphones, EQ and power, each explained in plain terms, with the research on what loudness does to guests.
props.meta_description: Why the toast gets lost and the back tables can't hear: how volume, echo, speaker placement, microphones, EQ and power decide how an event sounds, and what we ask before we quote.
props.llms_description: This is a guide to how a venue's acoustics and sound setup shape a private event, from an agency that books live musicians in Colorado. It covers volume (voices start rising at about 57 dB; field studies on how loud music changes drinking, ordering and taste), frequency (bass travels through walls, consonants are absorbed by a crowd), echo and speaker placement (reverberation blurs speech; halving the distance to a listener adds 6 dB), wattage and headroom (doubling power adds only 3 dB), the toast microphone and announcement clarity (speech needs to sit 10 to 15 dB above the background), EQ as subtraction, and power (a 15-amp circuit gives about 1,800 watts; ask the venue for a dedicated 20-amp circuit). It ends with the questions Signet asks before quoting.

hero.alt: A guest raising a champagne flute during a toast at a reception, the crowd soft behind it.

items.text: Past about 57 decibels guests start raising their voices, and the whole space climbs. Dinner music has to sit under that line; the dance floor comes up later.
Speaker count and placement do more than wattage. Doubling the power adds three decibels; halving the distance to a listener adds six.
The toast microphone, a dedicated power circuit and a hand on the volume are agreed with the planner and the venue before the date, so nobody negotiates it at 9:40.

props.html:
Somebody who matters stands up with a microphone in front of two hundred people, and the first sound in the ballroom is a squeal from the speakers. They flinch, step back, start again at half the voice, and the tables along the window catch every third word.

Nobody at that event remembers the second set. Everybody remembers the toast they couldn't hear.

Most of what goes wrong with live music at an event starts in the space, before anyone plays a note. A wall of glass, a twenty-foot ceiling, speakers sized for a bar, a microphone handed to someone who has never held one, and a single outlet shared with the coffee urns.

Most agencies send a video, a song list and a quote, and the space gets figured out at four in the afternoon on the day. We start with the space: how loud, which frequencies, how much echo, how much power, which microphone, and how far a voice has to carry. That is the terrain this covers.

props.text: Volume is a decision about conversation

props.html:
Every host has a number in mind for how loud the band should be. The question underneath it is who needs to talk, and when. (If you want the number itself, we've written it down.)

Here is the mechanism. When the background in a space passes roughly 57 decibels, people start raising their voices to be understood. Pasquale Bottalico's lab measured the tipping point at about that level, and found each extra decibel of noise adds another third to a half of a decibel to every voice in the space. Two hundred guests do that at once, and the level in the ballroom climbs until nobody can talk any louder. Braxton Boren at American University calls it a tragedy of the commons: the quiet is a shared resource, and every table takes a little more of it.

That climb is a big part of why noise was the number-one complaint in Zagat's 2018 national dining survey.

props.alt: A horizontal bar chart of measured sound levels from 50 to 90 decibels, with a dashed line at 57 decibels marked where voices start rising.
props.caption: Where everyday spaces sit against the 57 dB line.

props.html:
Loudness also changes what guests do. In two French bars, turning the music from 72 to 88 decibels moved the average from 2.6 drinks to 3.4 and cut the time per beer from about 14.5 minutes to 11.5 (more on that study here). In a Stockholm café, 70-decibel music produced about 20 percent more orders of the heavy items on the menu than 55-decibel music did. And a University of Manchester study found loud background noise made food taste less sweet and less salty. Your caterer's work is partly in the hands of whoever sets the level.

Older guests feel all of this first. Adults over 60 with ordinary hearing need speech a few decibels further above the background than younger adults do to follow it. A Washington planner told Washingtonian she started leaving earplugs on the tables for older guests because the volume complaints never stopped.

props.text: The earplugs are a workaround for a decision somebody else made.

props.html: So we set a level for dinner and a different one for dancing, and we agree on both before the night. Dinner sits under the conversation. The dance floor comes up when the floor opens. The oldest guest at the farthest table is the person we set dinner for.

props.alt: Couples dancing close together on a dim ballroom floor, in black and white.
props.caption: The second level of the night. It arrives when the floor opens, and never during dinner.

props.text: Low notes travel through walls. Consonants vanish into the crowd.

props.html:
Two things leave a speaker: the part you feel and the part you understand. Bass and kick drum sit below about 150 hertz, and those waves are long enough to pass through walls, roll down a corridor and arrive in the ballroom next door as a thump with no music attached. That thump is the complaint your catering manager gets.

Speech lives higher up. The consonants that tell "fifteen" from "sixteen" sit mostly between two and four kilohertz, and those waves are short, easily absorbed, and the first thing a crowd soaks up. Two hundred guests in wool and cotton are a wall of absorption that was missing at sound check, which is why a mix that sounded fine in an empty ballroom at three turns muddy at eight.

Surfaces pull in the other direction. Glass, marble and polished concrete throw the high end straight back at the guests, so everything feels harsh at a level that would be comfortable on carpet. A carpeted ballroom with drapes does the reverse: the highs vanish into the fabric and the low end hangs there with nothing to tame it.

props.alt: Long wooden tables set for a wedding under a glass roof, with greenery overhead and light pouring in.
props.caption: Glass overhead and tile underfoot. Beautiful at noon, bright and harsh at eight, and often no place for a subwoofer.

props.html: So whether a cocktail hour in a glass atrium needs a subwoofer at all is a real question, and the answer is often no. We decide that from the materials, before the truck is packed.

props.text: Echo, and where the speakers point

props.html:
Every space holds sound for a moment after the source stops. Acousticians call it reverberation time, and it runs from under a second in a treated ballroom to two or three seconds in a stone church or a glass atrium. In a long tail, each syllable is still ringing when the next one arrives, and the consonants that carry meaning blur together. Less reverberation means more of the speech gets understood; Bottalico's group showed it again in a 2025 study of university dining halls.

What a venue is built from is fixed by the time we arrive. What we control is where the sound starts and where it is pointed. Speakers aimed across a hall at a glass wall set the whole space ringing. Speakers aimed at people, raised to head height and brought closer to the tables, put most of the energy into bodies and clothing, which absorb it. Halving the distance between a speaker and a listener adds six decibels for that listener without touching the volume knob, which is why one extra pair of small speakers at the back of a long hall beats a bigger pair at the front almost every time.

props.alt: Two top-down diagrams of a long hall with twelve tables. Left, one large pair of speakers at the front: 92 decibels at the first table and 72 at the last. Right, two modest pairs, one at the front and one halfway back: 80 decibels at the first table and 78 at the last.
props.caption: Two ways to cover the same hall. The gap between the first table and the last is the point; the exact levels are illustrative.

props.html: A 2020 study that simulated restaurants found absorbers placed vertically and close to the diners did more for speech than the same treatment on the ceiling. Bodies are vertical absorbers close to the diners. Two hundred guests walk in and the space changes.

Watts are the number on the box, so watts are what people ask about. Start with what the number buys. Doubling the power adds three decibels, which most listeners barely register. Making something sound twice as loud takes about ten times the power. A thousand-watt speaker and a two-thousand-watt speaker in the same spot are closer than the price tags suggest.

What the extra power actually buys is headroom: the gap between how hard the speakers are working and their limit. A speaker running near its limit distorts, and distortion is what people mean when they say something sounds loud, even at a moderate level. The same level from a speaker with power to spare sounds clean, and clean sound carries further at a lower volume.

props.alt: A stack of old PA speakers and cabinets of different sizes against a white wall.
props.caption: The number on the box. Doubling it adds three decibels.

props.html: So the first table should not be paying in volume for the last table to hear. Count and placement do more than size. Two moderate speakers set well, plus a small second pair for the back of a long hall, cover two hundred guests more evenly than one enormous pair at the front. We size the speakers to the headcount and the dimensions of the space, and we would rather bring a fourth speaker than turn up a second one.

props.text: The toast microphone is the most important piece of equipment in the building

props.alt: A vintage microphone on a stand in front of tall windows in a wood-paneled space.
props.caption: Four minutes that cannot be redone, on one microphone, in front of a wall of glass.

props.html:
A wedding has maybe four minutes that cannot be redone, and all four happen on a handheld microphone in the hands of someone who has never held one. The same is true of the CEO's thank-you at the holiday party and the founder's remarks at the client dinner.

Three things go wrong with a voice on a microphone, and all three are preventable. The person holds it at their chest and the level drops by half. They drift toward a loudspeaker and the sound squeals. The band's dinner level is still up under the words, and the back of the hall hears music with a voice somewhere inside it.

Speech needs to sit about ten to fifteen decibels above whatever is underneath it to be understood without effort, and older listeners need a little more than that. So for every toast there is a hand on the volume, the music comes all the way down, and a level for the human voice is set before guests arrive and tested from the spot where the toasts will be given. The microphone is handed over by a person who says, in one sentence, hold it here, right at your chin. A second microphone is switched on and within reach.

The announcement that the shuttle leaves at eleven gets the same treatment. Miss it and the night ends with sixty guests on a curb.

Every space adds something to the sound that was never played. A ballroom corner builds up a boom around 120 hertz. A glass wall puts a ring around two and a half kilohertz. The instinct when something sounds unclear is to turn it up, and turning it up makes the boom and the ring louder along with everything else.

Equalization is the set of controls that pull those frequencies back down. Cut the boom and the bass tightens at the same volume. Cut the ring and the words come forward without anyone touching the level. That is the difference between loud and clear, and clear at 65 decibels does more for a dinner than loud at 80.

The microphone gets the same treatment before anyone arrives: raise it until it starts to squeal, find the frequency that rings, cut it, repeat. Twenty minutes of that is what makes a handheld safe in the hands of someone who has never used one.

props.text: Power: the outlet behind the band is shared with the coffee urn

props.html:
A standard 15-amp circuit delivers about 1,800 watts before the breaker trips. A 20-amp circuit gives about 2,400. A single coffee urn draws somewhere around 1,000 to 1,500 watts on its own. Electric chafing warmers, a photo booth printer and a wall of string lights all pull from somewhere, and in many ballrooms the outlets along one wall share a circuit with the outlets along the next, or with the catering line behind the partition.

Put powered speakers, a mixer and a keyboard amplifier on the same circuit as the coffee service and the breaker trips in the middle of the first dance. Put them on a circuit shared with the lighting dimmers and there is a hum under everything all night.

So power comes up in the first conversation with the venue. We ask for a dedicated 20-amp circuit where the band will stand, two if the space allows, and we ask where the panel is and who has the key. Long cable runs get heavy enough gauge that the voltage holds at the far end. Where the outlets are is the first thing we look for on a walkthrough, before the view. (The venue's form will ask about stage size and insurance too; that's covered here.)

props.text: What we ask before we quote

props.html:
We ask how many guests are coming, what the walls and floor are made of and how high the ceiling is, where the toasts will be given from and where the oldest guests will sit, where the outlets are and what else is on them, which hours of the night are for talking and which are for dancing, and whether there is another event on the other side of the wall.

From those answers we decide which speakers to bring, where they point, whether a subwoofer comes at all, and what the two levels of the night will be. All of it gets agreed before the date, with the planner and the venue, so nobody is negotiating volume with a bandleader at 9:40 while the client's mother asks for the fourth time.

On the night, dinner sits under the conversation. Every toast gets a hand on the volume and a second microphone within reach. The floor comes up when the floor opens.

The grandmother at the table by the window hears every word of the toast, and stays for the cake.
